<reason>Both sides argued competently, but PRO (B) built the more incisive substantive case. B's zero-sum boost argument (algorithmically manufactured scarcity, "disclosure to the buyer is not disclosure to the person demoted") was a sharp, largely original mechanism that CON never squarely rebutted—CON's reply that boosts are "just like sponsored search" ignored B's specific point that the platform controls and can throttle the organic baseline. B also narrowed the motion effectively via the "when" clause and pressed CON into a genuine dilemma in the Pressure Questions round (does a platform with clear internal proof of harm have any duty?), forcing CON into an answer ("No... no clean trigger") that read, fairly, as a concession that no obligation exists even in the clearest cases. CON's best material—vagueness of standard, market competition as discipline, swipe mechanics as legitimate filtering—remained live and CON's closing did meaningfully complicate B's "one word ended the debate" framing by exposing a real disanalogy in the restaurant/doctor comparisons (contested tradeoffs vs. an uncontested floor). That closing rejoinder narrows the gap, but it doesn't fully answer B's manufactured-scarcity point on boosts, which stands as an unrebutted harm mechanism supporting the proposition. B's opening being clipped for length is a real execution cost, but not enough to offset B's overall sharper mechanisms and more effective use of the pressure round.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 zero-sum boost argument ("my boost is literally your suppression... disclosure to the purchaser is not disclosure to the person being demoted") combined with the Pressure Questions trap forcing CON's "no clean trigger" answer in Rebuttal 2 was the most decisive exchange; CON never fully neutralized either.</best_rebuttal>
